s9.quote: Friends, countrymen, my last farewell I make;
s9.note: This is a kommos, a lament sung between an actor and the Chorus, and it is the first time Antigone sings. Storr's 'Friends, countrymen' is warmer than the Greek, where she calls them πολῖται (_politai_, "citizens", l. 806) of her father's land and her first word is _horate_, "look at me". The woman who has spoken all play of family and the dead now addresses the city and asks it to watch. Her last words in the scene will be the same demand: λεύσσετε (_leussete_, "look", l. 940).

s9.quote: One last fond, lingering, longing look I take
s9.note: Storr piles three adjectives where the Greek is spare: νεάταν ὁδὸν (_neatan hodon_, "the last road", l. 806) and then νέατον (_neaton_, "last") again for the sunlight, the same word twice. For once the Victorian excess seems right to me in spirit. This is the woman who told Ismene in [[s1]] that death would be a fine thing and told Creon in [[s5]] that it would be a gain, and she cannot take her eyes off the day. I do not think that is inconsistency. The courage was real, and so is the cost, which she is counting only now that nobody can call it a retreat.

s9.quote: For Death who puts to sleep both young and old
s9.note: The Greek has one compound, παγκοίτας (_pankoitas_, "who lays all to bed", l. 810), an epithet of Hades. The Chorus has just used it of her destination at the close of [[s8]], calling it the bridal chamber "where all are laid to rest", so she is picking up their word. Storr's 'puts to sleep' keeps the gentleness but loses the bed, and the bed matters: the whole scene turns on the confusion of marriage bed and grave.

s9.quote: And beckons me to Acheron’s dark fold,
s9.note: 'Beckons' is far too mild. The Greek is ζῶσαν ἄγει (_zosan agei_, "leads me, living", l. 810): Hades is taking her alive, and _agein_ is the ordinary verb for a bridegroom leading his bride home. Watch that verb through the scene. Hades leads her here, Creon is its subject at l. 916, and her last cry at l. 939 is ἄγομαι (_agomai_, "I am being led"). By then the bridegroom and the king have become one figure.

s9.quote: No youths have sung the marriage song for me,
s9.note: An Athenian wedding and an Athenian funeral looked alike: a procession by torchlight, a song, a washed and adorned body, a journey to a new house. A girl who died unmarried was said to have married Hades, as Persephone did. Antigone works through the list of what she has been denied (the hymn at the door, the hymn at the bed) and finds that the other ceremony supplies every item. Remember that she has a bridegroom, and that Haemon will be found with his arms round her in that chamber in [[s13]].

s9.quote: ’Tis Death I wed.
s9.note: The Greek is blunter and stranger: Ἀχέροντι νυμφεύσω (_Acheronti nympheuso_, "I shall be bride to Acheron", l. 815). Her husband is a river in the underworld. Storr's 'Death' turns it into an abstraction, and the earlier 'unwed wife' is his own paradox, not hers. Notice that Haemon's name does not occur anywhere in this scene. Whatever the Chorus sang about Eros in [[s8]], she laments marriage and children as a state she has lost, never a particular man.

s9.quote: Great and glorious, to the dead.
s9.note: κλεινὴ (_kleine_, "famous", l. 817) and ἔπαινον (_epainon_, "praise") are the elders' answer to her grief. It is the consolation one offers a warrior, and they have nothing else to offer. Is it kind? I think it is meant kindly and is tone-deaf. She asked to be looked at and pitied, and they tell her she will be well spoken of. It is also the first time these men have conceded in public that what she did is praiseworthy, which bears out Haemon's report in [[s7]] of what the city says under its breath.

s9.quote: Thou the sword’s edge hast not tasted,
s9.note: The elders reckon the ways people usually die, wasting sickness and what they grimly call the wages of swords, and observe that she has avoided both. It is the reasoning of old men who have seen many deaths. To a young woman about to be walled up it can only sound like being told she is lucky.

s9.quote: Freely thou alone shalt go
s9.note: Storr's 'freely' stands for the most discussed word in the scene: αὐτόνομος (_autonomos_, "living by one's own law", l. 821). It is a political term, used of cities that keep their own laws, and so far as I know this is its earliest surviving application to a person. A _nomos_ of her own is exactly what Creon accused her of setting against the city's. Do the elders intend praise or blame? I think the word is honestly double: of her own free choice and a law unto herself. Our 'autonomy' descends from it, and has lost the warning.

s9.quote: Living to the dead below.
s9.note: The Greek stresses that she is unique: μόνη (_mone_, "alone", l. 821) of mortals she will go down to Hades alive. The elders offer this as her distinction. It is in fact the horror of the sentence, since she will be neither buried nor alive. Creon has left one corpse above ground and is sending one living body under it, and that inversion is precisely the charge Teiresias will bring against him in [[s11]].

s9.quote: Nay, but the piteous tale I’ve heard men tell
s9.note: She does not answer the consolation at all. Offered glory, she reaches for a precedent of her own choosing, and it is the saddest one she knows: the superlative _lygrotatan_, "most wretched", is the first thing she says about it. A tutor's question: why does she want a mythical parallel at this moment? I think because nobody on stage will mourn her, and a myth is company.

s9.quote: Of Tantalus’ doomed child,
s9.note: Niobe, daughter of Tantalus, boasted that her children outnumbered Leto's, lost them all to Apollo and Artemis, and turned to stone on Mount Sipylus, still weeping. Antigone calls her τὰν Φρυγίαν ξέναν (_tan Phrygian xenan_, "the Phrygian stranger", l. 823), which Storr drops. Niobe came to Thebes as a foreign bride, the wife of Amphion, so the comparison is local and it introduces the idea of the outsider that Antigone will shortly turn on herself. It is an odd choice all the same: the woman who will have no children picks the great bereaved mother, and a woman punished for a boast.

s9.quote: That clung like ivy wild,
s9.note: Storr has the simile backwards. In the Greek the stone is the ivy: κισσὸς (_kissos_, "ivy", l. 825) is what the growth of rock is compared to, and the verb is δάμασεν (_damasen_, "subdued", l. 826). The rock crept over Niobe and overpowered her as ivy overpowers a wall. _Damazein_ is also used for breaking in an animal and for taking a wife, so the stone is one more bridegroom.

s9.quote: While on her frozen breast the tears aye flow—
s9.note: The participle for Niobe is τακομέναν (_takomenan_, "melting, wasting away", l. 826): rain and snow never leave her and she dissolves in tears while remaining stone. Keep the verb in mind. It returns for the husband who might have "wasted" in death at l. 906 and for the blinded sons in the next ode. What Antigone envies in Niobe, I think, is that her grief is permanent and visible, a monument that weeps. Her own tomb will be sealed and seen by no one.

s9.quote: Her fate is mine.
s9.note: The Greek is more exact: a δαίμων (_daimon_, "divine power", l. 831) is putting her to bed, κατευνάζει (_kateunazei_), "most like" Niobe. The bed again. And she says a god is doing it. She does not say Creon, and this is the first moment in the play where she attributes her end to something larger than one man's decree.

s9.quote: She was sprung of gods, divine,
s9.note: The rebuke. θεός (_theos_, "a god", l. 834) and θεογεννής (_theogennes_, "god-born") are set against βροτοὶ (_brotoi_, "mortals", l. 835) and _thnetogeneis_, "mortal-born". Strictly Niobe was no goddess, only a granddaughter of Zeus, so the elders overstate their case to make it. It is a pedant's correction delivered to a girl on the way to her death. But see what they hear in her comparison: a claim to rank with the divine. Niobe was destroyed for exactly that, so the correction carries a warning too.

s9.quote: Like renown with gods to gain
s9.note: Having corrected her, they try to give the comparison back as a compliment. It is a great thing, they say, for one who has perished even to be said to share the lot of the ἰσοθέοις (_isotheois_, "the godlike", l. 837). σύγκληρα (_synklera_, "sharing an allotment") answers the word she used when she said she had no share in wedding songs. Their only currency is still reputation. Storr's 'recompenses all thy pain' promises more than the Greek, which says only that it is no small thing to hear.

s9.quote: Hers in life and death thy doom.
s9.note: So does the Chorus console or mock? I take them to be sincere and inept. They are old men who admire fame, fear power and believe in limits, and every consolation they offer is true by their lights. What they will not do is the one thing she came out for, which is to weep for her and say she was wronged. They did weep, at the end of [[s8]], before she spoke. Once she claims a likeness to Niobe they begin to judge, and judgment is all she gets from them until she is gone.

s9.quote: Alack, alack! Ye mock me. Is it meet
s9.note: 'Meet' means fitting. Her word is γελῶμαι (_gelomai_, "I am laughed at", l. 839), the thing a Sophoclean hero can least endure, and she follows it with ὑβρίζεις (_hybrizeis_, "you outrage me", l. 840). Both words have been used before, against her: in [[s5]] Creon said her _hybris_ was doubled because she laughed over what she had done. She now turns his two charges on the elders. And she adds ἐπίφαντον (_epiphanton_, "still in plain view"): could you not have waited until I was gone?

s9.quote: Ye lordly rulers of a lordly race.
s9.note: The Greek is ὦ πόλις (_o polis_, "O city", l. 841) and then πολυκτήμονες ἄνδρες (_polyktemones andres_, "men of many possessions"). Storr's 'lordly' hides the edge. She is addressing the propertied men of Thebes, the people with something to lose, and that is a diagnosis of why they have not spoken up. Note _andres_ too: in this play the word 'men' is seldom neutral.

s9.quote: O fount of Dirce, wood-embowered plain
s9.note: Since the citizens will not be her witnesses she appoints the landscape: she takes the springs of Dirce and the grove of Thebes as ξυμμάρτυρας (_xymmartyras_, "fellow witnesses", l. 845). These are the places the Chorus sang of in the victory ode of [[s2]], Dirce's streams and Thebes of the many chariots. She is claiming the city of that song, the physical and ancestral Thebes, over the heads of the men who now speak for it.

s9.quote: the cruel laws that now have wrought my bane,
s9.note: 'Cruel' is Storr's. The Greek is the exclamation οἵοις νόμοις (_hoiois nomois_, "by what sort of laws", l. 846), and the contempt is in the pronoun. This is the play's contest over _nomos_ in two words. In [[s5]] she set the gods' unwritten _nomima_ above a mortal's proclamation, and she has not moved: Creon's decree is called a law only with a sneer. She also calls the tomb a grave of a new and unheard-of kind, which is fair, since Creon invented the punishment in [[s7]].

s9.quote: The friends who show no pity in my need!
s9.note: φίλων ἄκλαυτος (_philon aklautos_, "unwept by friends", l. 846). _Philoi_ are one's own people, kin first, and the word has carried her whole case since [[s1]]. Is the complaint true? Ismene offered to die with her and was refused, and Haemon has just broken with his father for her sake. She seems not to know about Haemon, and she has cut Ismene out of the family. Her isolation is real, but she built some of it herself.

s9.quote: And alien midst the living and the dead.
s9.note: The word is μέτοικος (_metoikos_, l. 851), the Athenian term for a resident foreigner, someone who lives in a city without belonging to it. She will be a metic everywhere, housed with neither the living nor the dead. Every Athenian in the theatre knew exactly what status that was. She uses it again at l. 867, and Creon picks it up coldly at l. 890. It also answers her own 'Phrygian stranger': Niobe was a foreigner in Thebes, and Antigone will be one in both worlds.

s9.quote: In thy boldness over-rash
s9.note: From here the Chorus sings in lyric with her and its tone hardens from consolation to verdict. You went, they say, to the furthest edge of θράσους (_thrasous_, "daring, rashness", l. 853). _Thrasos_ is courage seen from the disapproving side. They still call her τέκνον (_teknon_, "child", l. 855), which Storr omits, and the tenderness of that word laid over the severity of the judgment is the Chorus's whole position.

s9.quote: ’Gainst high Justice’ altar stair.
s9.note: Δίκας βάθρον (_Dikas bathron_, "the pedestal of Justice", l. 854), with the verb προσέπεσες (_prosepeses_, l. 855). The verb can mean you fell against it, like someone stumbling, or you fell before it, like a suppliant, and some readers have wanted the second so as to make the elders kinder. I think collision is meant. But ask which Justice. In [[s5]] Antigone claimed the _Dike_ who lives with the gods below as her authority, and the elders now tell her she has run into the very power she invoked.

s9.quote: Thou a father’s guild dost bear.
s9.note: 'Guild' is a misprint for 'guilt'. The Greek is vaguer than Storr: πατρῷον (_patroion_, "of your father, ancestral", l. 856) and ἆθλον (_athlon_, "ordeal, contest"), which she is paying out in full. This is the explanation the elders gave in [[s6]], the ruin that runs down the house of Labdacus, now said to her face. It lets them hold two views at once: she chose this, and it was laid on her. It also spares them from having to say anything about Creon.

s9.quote: At this thou touchest my most poignant pain,
s9.note: ἔψαυσας (_epsausas_, "you have touched", l. 858) the sorest of her μερίμνας (_merimnas_, "cares"). She does not dispute the diagnosis. The lament for her father she calls τριπόλιστον (_tripoliston_, l. 859), thrice-ploughed, turned over and over like a field. In a family whose disaster was a son sowing where he was sown, and after Creon's remark in [[s5]] that there are other fields for Haemon to plough, the farming metaphor is hard to hear as innocent.

s9.quote: Woe worth the monstrous marriage-bed where lay
s9.note: The first word of her cry over the marriage bed is ἆται (_atai_, "ruins, delusions", l. 865). _Ate_ was the refrain of [[s6]], the ruin a god sends on a house, and here she accepts the Chorus's own term for her family. The union she calls by a word built on _auto-_ (_autogenneta_, "self-engendered"): a mother lying with a son she bore herself. This play is full of _auto-_ compounds for the family folded in on itself, from the _autadelphos_ of the first line onward. Her lament for the marriage she will not have runs straight back to the marriage that produced her.

s9.quote: To meet them as an alien there below;
s9.note: μέτοικος (_metoikos_, l. 867) again, and this time it contradicts everything she has said. From [[s1]] on, the dead of her family were the people she belonged with, and she would lie beside them as a loved one. Now she expects to be a resident alien even there, ἀραῖος ἄγαμος (_araios agamos_, "accursed, unmarried"). I take this as the lowest point of her confidence. It should be weighed against the hope she voices at l. 897: she holds both.

s9.quote: And thee, O brother, in marriage ill-bestead,
s9.note: The brother is Polyneices and the marriage is his to Argeia, daughter of Adrastus of Argos, the alliance that gave him an army to bring against Thebes. So there are three ruinous marriages in this stanza: her parents', her brother's, and her own to Acheron. In this family marriage is how catastrophe travels.

s9.quote: ’Twas thy dead hand that dealt me this death-blow.
s9.note: The Greek sets the two participles against each other: dead, you killed me while I still lived, with the heavy epic verb κατήναρές (_katenares_, "you slew", l. 871), a word for killing in battle. She has not said anything like this before. In [[s5]] the burial was a glory and a duty, and here, for one line, it is something her brother did to her. It is not regret, since she never wishes it undone. It is the first admission that the dead take as well as receive, and the play ends with Creon as a living man destroyed by his dead.

s9.quote: Religion has her chains, ’tis true,
s9.note: σέβειν (_sebein_, "to show reverence", l. 872) is εὐσέβειά τις (_eusebeia tis_, "a kind of piety"). The little word _tis_ is grudging: reverence of your sort is piety of a sort. Still, this is the Chorus conceding in so many words that what she did was _eusebeia_, the virtue she will claim with her last breath. Storr's 'chains' is his own invention and makes the concession sound like a complaint against religion, which it is not.

s9.quote: The powers who hold by might the sway.
s9.note: κράτος (_kratos_, "power", l. 873) twice in a line: for the man whose business power is, power is παραβατὸν (_parabaton_, "to be transgressed", l. 874) in no way at all. Read it carefully. The elders do not say Creon is right. They say power does not tolerate being crossed, which is an observation about power, and for a moral judgment it is close to an evasion. One line for piety, two for power: that ratio is as exact a statement of the Chorus's position as the play gives.

s9.quote: A self-willed rebel, thou must die.
s9.note: The Greek has no 'rebel' and no 'must die'. It says your αὐτόγνωτος (_autognotos_, "self-determined", l. 875) ὀργά (_orga_, "temper") destroyed you. _Autognotos_ is the partner of _autonomos_ fifty lines earlier, a temper that takes counsel only of itself, and the ambiguity of that word is now settled on the side of blame. _Orge_ is no less Creon's passion: in [[s3]] he warns these same elders to stop before they fill him with it. And the tense is past. They speak of her as already destroyed.

s9.quote: Unwept, unwed, unfriended, hence I go,
s9.note: She answers nothing. Three privatives stand in a row: ἄκλαυτος, ἄφιλος, ἀνυμέναιος (_aklautos, aphilos, anymenaios_, "unwept, friendless, without wedding song", l. 876). Storr keeps the hammering and shuffles the order. Then ἄγομαι (_agomai_, "I am led"), the bride's verb in the passive. The dialogue with the Chorus is over, and I think she has stopped expecting anything from them.

s9.quote: No longer may I see the day’s bright eye;
s9.note: The sun is the ἱερὸν ὄμμα (_hieron omma_, "sacred eye", l. 878) of the torch of day, and the word Storr renders 'may' is θέμις (_themis_, "what is right, what is sanctioned", l. 880). It is no longer _themis_ for her to look at the light. That is a bitter use of a religious word by someone who holds that everything she did was sanctioned. The Chorus greeted this same sun in [[s2]] as the eye of golden day rising on a rescued Thebes.

s9.quote: Not one friend left to share my bitter woe,
s9.note: οὐδεὶς φίλων (_oudeis philon_, "none of my own", l. 882) groans for a fate that is ἀδάκρυτον (_adakryton_, "untearful", l. 881). This is exactly the state she refused to leave Polyneices in. In [[s1]] the edict's cruelty was that he should lie unwept and unburied, and by curing that she has taken it on herself. She gave her brother a mourner and has none.

s9.quote: If wail and lamentation aught availed
s9.note: Creon cuts in with spoken verse after seventy lines of song, and the drop in register is the point. Whether he has stood there throughout or comes back on now is disputed, and I prefer to imagine him present and silent, so that the elders' deference to power is performed under his eye. His opening is a sneer in the form of a proverb: nobody would ever stop his ἀοιδὰς καὶ γόους (_aoidas kai goous_, "songs and wailings", l. 883) before death if it were allowed. He treats mourning as a delaying tactic, as he has all along.

s9.quote: Leave her alone at liberty to die,
s9.note: The Greek is ἄφετε μόνην ἔρημον (_aphete monen eremon_, "leave her alone, deserted", l. 887), whether she wishes to die or to go on living entombed. Storr's 'at liberty' is his, but it catches the grotesque tone. Creon is arranging matters so that her death will look like her own choice. In the event she takes him at his word and hangs herself, and that act, which he thinks keeps his hands clean, is what kills his son.

s9.quote: Are guiltless as concerns this maiden’s blood,
s9.note: ἁγνοὶ (_hagnoi_, "pure", l. 889) is a ritual term: free of _miasma_, the pollution of bloodshed. This is why she is walled up with a little food and not stoned as the edict first threatened. Leave a kinswoman to starve and technically no one has killed her. It is a legalism addressed to the gods by a man who scoffed in [[s3]] at the idea that the gods could care for this corpse. Teiresias will tell him in [[s11]] that the city's altars are polluted because of him. And he calls her κόρην (_koren_, "girl"). He does not address her once in this scene.

s9.quote: Only on earth no lodging shall she find.
s9.note: He has been listening. She called herself a _metoikos_ twice, and he answers that she will be deprived of her μετοικίας (_metoikias_, "residence as an alien", l. 890) up here. He takes her bitterest word and makes it administrative: her permit to stay is withdrawn. It also concedes something he may not notice, that she was never more than a lodger in his Thebes.

s9.quote: O grave, O bridal bower, O prison house
s9.note: The speech opens with a triple address: τύμβος (_tymbos_, "tomb", l. 891), νυμφεῖον (_nympheion_, "bridal chamber"), and a dwelling that is κατασκαφὴς (_kataskaphes_, "dug deep") and ἀείφρουρος (_aeiphrouros_, "keeping watch for ever", l. 892). Tomb, bride's room and guardhouse are one place. She has stopped singing and now speaks in the iambics of argument. That change matters for what follows: this is a speech of reasons, addressed to the dead, not a continuation of the lament.

s9.quote: Of kinsfolk, Persephassa’s guests long dead,
s9.note: Persephassa is Persephone, the girl Hades carried off to be his bride, so the hostess of this house is the pattern for Antigone's own fate. She says she is going πρὸς τοὺς ἐμαυτῆς (_pros tous emautes_, "to my own", l. 893). And she calls herself λοισθία (_loisthia_, "the last", l. 895) of them, which leaves no room for Ismene.

s9.quote: And yet good hope is mine that I shall find
s9.note: Against the fear of being an alien among the dead she sets a hope, and the Greek says she nurses it: ἐλπίσιν (_elpisin_, "hopes", l. 897) with the verb for feeding. She will come φίλη (_phile_, "dear", l. 898) to her father, προσφιλὴς (_prosphiles_) to her mother, φίλη again to her brother. This returns to her promise in [[s1]] that she would lie with Polyneices, dear with one who is dear. The order is father, mother, brother, the family she was born into. No husband, and nothing about Thebes.

s9.quote: From with these hands, I laved and decked your limbs
s9.note: 'From' is a misprint for 'For'. The word is αὐτόχειρ (_autocheir_, "with my own hand", l. 900): she washed, dressed and poured χοὰς (_choas_, "libations", l. 902) for father, mother and brother. That brother, addressed as κασίγνητον κάρα (_kasigneton kara_, "brother's dear head", l. 899), must be Eteocles, since Polyneices is named next. It is the idiom of the play's first line, where Ismene was a dear sister's head. _Autocheir_ will come back in [[s13]] for people who die by their own hands.

s9.quote: I paid due rites, and this my recompense!
s9.note: The verb is ἄρνυμαι (_arnymai_, "I win, I earn", l. 903), the word for carrying off a prize or a wage. For tending your body, Polyneices, such are my winnings. The play's long argument about _kerdos_, gain, lies behind it: Creon thinks everyone acts for profit, and in [[s5]] she called an early death a gain. Here she audits the account and the tone is not triumphant.

s9.quote: Yet am I justified in wisdom’s eyes.
s9.note: Here begins the most disputed passage in Sophocles, ll. 904 to 920. The line says she honoured him rightly in the eyes of τοῖς φρονοῦσιν εὖ (_tois phronousin eu_, "those who think well", l. 904). _Phronein_ is the play's contested word: Creon, Haemon and Teiresias each claim good sense and the last lines of the play award it to nobody on stage. She appeals over the heads of the Chorus, who have just denied her that quality, to a jury of the right-minded who are not present. The cautious reading is that everything from here to 'a living grave' may be an actor's addition. I do not think it is.

s9.quote: For even had it been some child of mine,
s9.note: The case against. In [[s5]] she appealed to laws of the gods that bind everyone and say the dead must be buried. Here she says she would not have done it for a husband or a child, which seems to shrink a principle into a preference. The argument is lifted from Herodotus, where the wife of Intaphernes, allowed by Darius to save one condemned relative, chooses her brother because a husband and children can be replaced. There it makes sense, because she is choosing whom to keep alive. Antigone's brother is already dead. Goethe told Eckermann he wished some scholar would prove the lines spurious, and Jebb bracketed them.

s9.quote: I had not wrought this deed despite the State.
s9.note: βίᾳ πολιτῶν (_biai politon_, "in defiance of the citizens", l. 907). This is Ismene's phrase from [[s1]], where she said she was not made to act in defiance of the citizens. It is a startling thing for Antigone to say, because in [[s5]] she insisted the citizens agreed with her and were only gagged by fear. Those who reject the passage count this as a further inconsistency. I read it as what the last hundred lines have taught her. The citizens were on stage, and they told her that her own temper destroyed her.

s9.quote: What is the law I call in aid? ’Tis thus
s9.note: She calls her reasoning a νόμου (_nomou_, "law", l. 908): in deference to what _nomos_ do I say this? So the _nomos_ she set against Creon's turns out, when spelled out, to be a rule about the irreplaceable. The husband who might have died is imagined with the verb ἐτήκετο (_eteketo_, "was wasting away", l. 906), Niobe's verb, used here of a corpse rotting as her brother's has been. The syntax of the next lines is awkward, and that awkwardness is one of the editors' complaints.

s9.quote: No second brother can be born for me.
s9.note: The case for. Aristotle quotes these lines in the Rhetoric as from the Antigone, to show how a speaker should give a reason when a claim sounds incredible, so the passage stood in the text within a century of Sophocles' death. Sophocles and Herodotus were contemporaries and by ancient report acquainted, and a borrowed story is not evidence of a second hand. Most recent editors keep the lines. And as a statement of fact about this house, with father, mother and both brothers dead, the line is simply how alone she is.

s9.quote: Thus by the law of conscience I was led
s9.note: 'Conscience' is Storr importing a Christian faculty. The Greek says only that she honoured him above all by such a νόμῳ (_nomoi_, "law", l. 914). My own view is that the passage is Sophocles' and that it tells the truth about her. She never buried a stranger. Her great speech in [[s5]] was made about a brother, and from her first line her loyalty has been to those of the same womb. What embarrasses readers is finding that the heroine of universal law was moved by a particular love. But a twenty-line cut would also heal rather neatly, from 'this my recompense' to 'what ordinance of heaven', so I hold the view without certainty.

s9.quote: By Creon guilty of a heinous crime.
s9.note: δεινὰ τολμᾶν (_deina tolman_, "to dare terrible things", l. 915). Both words come from the ode on man in [[s4]], where man is the most _deinon_ of creatures and the one who consorts with wrong for the sake of daring is to be cast out of the city. She puts the judgment in Creon's mouth and the vocabulary fits her exactly. Whether the ode was about her, about him, or about both is a question the play does not let you close.

s9.quote: A bride unwed, amerced of marriage-song
s9.note: 'Amerced' means fined, deprived. ἄλεκτρον, ἀνυμέναιον (_alektron, anymenaion_, "without marriage bed, without wedding song", l. 917) repeats the privatives of the lyric in plain speech, and she adds the rearing of a child, the only place she says she wanted one. That gives the replaceable-husband argument a sting people overlook. The woman who has just reasoned that husbands and children can be had again is counting them among what she has lost, a few lines later. That is not coldness. It is someone pricing what she paid.

s9.quote: By friends deserted to a living grave.
s9.note: ἔρημος πρὸς φίλων (_eremos pros philon_, "deserted by friends", l. 919) takes up the very word Creon used a moment ago when he ordered her left alone and deserted. And she goes living to the κατασκαφάς (_kataskaphas_, "dug-out chambers", l. 920) of the dead, the noun of the adjective that opened the speech. The disputed passage ends by closing the ring with the speech's first line, which is neat workmanship for an interpolator.

s9.quote: What ordinance of heaven have I transgressed?
s9.note: δαιμόνων δίκην (_daimonon diken_, "justice of the gods", l. 921). The Chorus told her she had crashed against the pedestal of Justice, and this is her reply, delayed by sixty lines. She asks it as a real question. In [[s5]] she knew what the gods' justice required. Now the gods have let her be led away, and she asks which of their laws she can have broken.

s9.quote: Hereafter can I look to any god
s9.note: Why should she still look to the gods, and which of them can she call as ξυμμάχων (_xymmachon_, "allies", l. 923)? The word is military: someone who fights at your side. No god does. This is the loneliest moment in the play and Sophocles does not soften it. The vindication comes, through Teiresias in [[s11]], but only after she has left the stage, and she dies without knowing she was right.

s9.quote: Alas, my piety is impious deemed.
s9.note: The Greek is harsher than 'deemed': by being pious, εὐσεβοῦσʼ (_eusebousa_), she has acquired δυσσέβειαν (_dyssebeian_, "impiety", l. 924), and the verb ἐκτησάμην (_ektesamen_) means got as a possession. Compare the 'sinless sinner' of [[s1]], her boast that she would commit a holy crime. Then she owned the crime and gloried in the holiness. Now the paradox is turned inside out and spoken without defiance: she has only the verdict.

s9.quote: I shall be taught by suffering my sin;
s9.note: If this is καλά (_kala_, "fine, right", l. 925) in the gods' eyes, then παθόντες (_pathontes_, "having suffered", l. 926) she would come to acknowledge, ξυγγνοῖμεν (_xyngnoimen_), that she has erred. It is the old idea of learning through suffering, and it is her one conditional admission that she might be wrong. Set it beside Creon, who in [[s13]] says he has learned, too late. She entertains the possibility before she is forced to. He never did.

s9.quote: No worse ills than the wrongs they do to me.
s9.note: It sounds like moderation and it is a curse: may they suffer no more than they are doing to me ἐκδίκως (_ekdikos_, "outside justice", l. 928). The verb for their error, ἁμαρτάνουσι (_hamartanousi_, l. 927), is the one Creon's judgment applied to her at l. 914. What they are doing to her is burying a living person among the dead, cut off from everyone she loves. Measure for measure, that is what Creon gets: by the end of [[s13]] the messenger calls him a breathing corpse. The prayer is granted exactly.

s9.quote: Drives like a gale the maiden still.
s9.note: The same ψυχῆς ῥιπαὶ (_psyches rhipai_, "gusts of the soul", l. 930) of the same ἀνέμων (_anemon_, "winds", l. 929) still hold her. That is the elders' whole response to forty lines of reasoning, doubt and prayer. They heard the curse at the end and nothing else. The storm comes from their own ode in [[s6]], where the ruin of the house was a swell driven by Thracian winds, and the north wind himself appears in the song they sing next.

s9.quote: Shall smart full sore for their delay.
s9.note: Creon's last words in her presence are a threat to the guards for βραδυτῆτος (_bradytetos_, "slowness", l. 932). He has not answered one thing she said, and in the whole scene he never speaks to her, only about her. His impatience is worth marking, because haste is his fault throughout: he is in a hurry to be rid of her now, and at the end of [[s11]] he will be in a hurry to undo it, and will get the order of his errands wrong.

s9.quote: Brings death most near.
s9.note: The manuscripts give this cry to Antigone and I see no reason to move it, though some editors have assigned it to the Chorus. If it is hers, it is the only moment in the play where the fact of death reaches her as fear, with no argument round it. It lasts two lines.

s9.quote: I have no comfort. What he saith,
s9.note: The speaker is disputed. Storr gives the couplet to the Chorus, and many editors give it to Creon: I offer you no encouragement to hope the sentence will not be carried out. The verb παραμυθοῦμαι (_paramythoumai_, "I console, I encourage", l. 935) suits either. In Creon's mouth it is a last turn of the knife. In the elders' mouths it is an honest confession that they have nothing left to say, and after the consolations of this scene I find that the more telling reading.

s9.quote: My fatherland, city of Thebes divine,
s9.note: She began the scene by addressing the citizens and ends by addressing the city itself, ἄστυ πατρῷον (_asty patroion_, "town of my fathers", l. 937), and the θεοὶ προγενεῖς (_theoi progeneis_, "ancestral gods", l. 938). The Theban royal house descends from gods, so these are literally her forebears. The girl who was told she was mortal and no Niobe goes out claiming the gods as family. It is also her answer to the notion that she is the city's enemy.

s9.quote: Look, puissant lords of Thebes, on me;
s9.note: She calls the elders κοιρανίδαι (_koiranidai_, "princes, ruling men", l. 940) of Thebes. It is a pointed title for men who have ruled nothing in this scene. If they are lords, then what is being done is being done by their leave. Just before it she says ἄγομαι (_agomai_) one last time and adds that she delays no longer, which takes Creon's taunt about slowness and makes the going her own act.

s9.quote: The last of all your royal house ye see.
s9.note: μούνην λοιπήν (_mounen loipen_, "the only one left", l. 941). Ismene is alive, inside the palace, a few yards away. Antigone told her in [[s5]] that she had chosen to live, and here she strikes her from the family for good. It is the harshest thing in the part. It is also in keeping with the argument about the brother: she counts as kin those to whom the debt is owed, and Ismene declined the debt.

s9.quote: Martyred by men of sin, undone.
s9.note: 'Martyred' and 'sin' are Storr's Christian colouring. The Greek is barer and angrier: οἷα πρὸς οἵων ἀνδρῶν (_hoia pros hoion andron_, "what things, from what sort of men", l. 942) I suffer. Hear ἀνδρῶν. Creon has said again and again that he will not be beaten by a woman, and her parting description of her judges is that they are men, and of what kind.

s9.quote: Such meed my piety hath won.
s9.note: 'Meed' means reward. Her last words in the play are τὴν εὐσεβίαν σεβίσασα (_ten eusebian sebisasa_, "for having revered reverence", l. 943), the noun and its own verb. The Chorus allowed her 'a kind of piety'. She leaves claiming the thing itself, twice in three words. What has it earned her? On stage, nothing: no sign from the gods, no mourner, no word from Creon. The play then spends its remaining third proving her right about the burial, and none of it reaches her. She does not appear again alive.

s10.quote: Like to thee that maiden bright,
s10.note: Antigone has just been led off and Creon, on the usual view, is still on stage, so the ode is sung over her absence and in front of her judge. The elders offer three stories of people of high birth who were shut up in stone or bronze. Ask of each what the prisoner shares with Antigone and what not. The first word is ἔτλα (_etla_, "she endured", l. 944): the lesson offered is endurance. The ode never says whether she was right.

s10.quote: Danae, in her brass-bound tower,
s10.note: Danae's father Acrisius shut her away because of a prophecy that her son would kill him. The Greek has χαλκοδέτοις αὐλαῖς (_chalkodetois aulais_, "bronze-bound halls", l. 945), a chamber rather than Storr's fairy-tale tower. What she gave up is the οὐράνιον φῶς (_ouranion phos_, "light of heaven", l. 944), the sunlight Antigone has just taken leave of. The likeness is close: a king's daughter, innocent, entombed by her own kin to prevent a marriage.

s10.quote: For a cell, her bridal bower.
s10.note: τυμβήρει θαλάμῳ (_tymberei thalamoi_, "a tomb-like chamber", l. 946). _Thalamos_ is the word for a bride's room, and it is the Chorus's own word for where Antigone was going at the end of [[s8]]. So the elders have absorbed her equation of tomb and bridal chamber and hand it back as myth. But here is the difference they do not state. Danae's tomb really did become a marriage chamber and she came out of it with a son. Antigone's is a bridal chamber only in metaphor, until Haemon dies in it.

s10.quote: And yet she sprang of royal line,
s10.note: τίμιος (_timios_, "honoured", l. 947) in her birth. This is the thread the elders use to tie the three stories together: none of these prisoners was saved by rank. It is a consoling moral only on the surface. A minute ago Antigone called on her ancestral gods and her royal blood, and the ode answers that blood has never helped anyone. The verb for Danae's confinement is κατεζεύχθη (_katezeuchthe_, "she was yoked down", l. 946), and the yoke will return for Lycurgus.

s10.quote: My child, like thine,
s10.note: The Greek doubles the address: ὦ παῖ παῖ (_o pai pai_, "child, child", l. 947). They called her child to her face only once, the _teknon_ of [[s9]], and they say it three times in this ode, now that she is out of hearing. The tenderness is real and it costs them nothing. That, I think, is the measure of this Chorus.

s10.quote: Of Zeus descending in a golden shower.
s10.note: Zeus reached Danae as a rain of gold and she bore Perseus. The Greek has her ταμιεύεσκε (_tamieueske_, "kept in store, was steward of", l. 950) the seed of Zeus that was χρυσορύτους (_chrysorytous_, "gold-flowing"), a housekeeper's verb, as if she were a treasury. So a god came to Danae in her prison. None comes to Antigone, who asked in [[s9]] which god she could still look to. The example, told to comfort, measures exactly what she has not been given.

s10.quote: Strange are the ways of Fate, her power
s10.note: Storr's 'strange' is δεινά (_deina_, "terrible, formidable", l. 951), the adjective that opened the ode on man in [[s4]]. There, nothing was more _deinon_ than man. Here the power that is _deina_ is μοιριδία (_moiridia_, "of fate, allotted"), with an indefinite _tis_: some power of destiny. The elders have reversed their own earlier song, and the reversal is the main thing this ode has to say.

s10.quote: Nor wealth, nor arms withstand, nor tower;
s10.note: The list is ὄλβος (_olbos_, "prosperity", l. 952), Ἄρης (_Ares_, war), πύργος (_pyrgos_, "a towered wall"), and black ships beaten by the sea. Set it beside [[s4]]: ships crossing the grey sea and the building of cities were man's proudest works there, and the only thing he could not escape was Hades. Now ships and city walls head the list of what cannot escape fate. Who in this play has wealth, an army and a walled city? Not Antigone.

s10.quote: Thus Dryas’ child, the rash Edonian King,
s10.note: Lycurgus, king of the Edonians in Thrace, tried to drive out Dionysus and his women. Storr's 'rash' is ὀξύχολος (_oxycholos_, "quick to anger", l. 955). The second example is a king, a man and guilty. It does not fit Antigone well, and it fits Creon very well: a sharp-tempered ruler who sets himself against a god and against inspired women. Did the elders intend that, with Creon listening? I think Sophocles did, and that the Chorus slides into it without quite knowing.

s10.quote: For words of high disdain
s10.note: κερτομίοις ὀργαῖς (_kertomiois orgais_, "jeering fits of temper", l. 956). ὀργαῖς is the word the elders fixed on Antigone when they said her self-willed _orge_ destroyed her, so verbally Lycurgus is tied to her. But jeering is not her manner, and it is Creon's: he taunted the Guard, Ismene, Haemon and Antigone herself, and in [[s11]] he will taunt a prophet. The stanza hangs between the two of them, and I do not think that is carelessness.

s10.quote: Did Bacchus to a rocky dungeon bring,
s10.note: πετρώδει (_petrodei_, "rocky", l. 957) and δεσμῷ (_desmoi_, "bond, prison"): the rock chamber is the outward link to Antigone's sentence. The verb is ζεύχθη (_zeuchthe_, "he was yoked", l. 955), the same root as Danae's. Creon complained in [[s3]] of citizens who would not keep their necks under the yoke. The yoke in this ode belongs to fate and to Dionysus, who is a god of Thebes and whom the Chorus will summon in [[s12]] to come and heal the city.

s10.quote: To cool the madness of a fevered brain.
s10.note: The image is of something dripping away: the δεινὸν (_deinon_, "terrible", l. 958) and ἀνθηρόν (_antheron_, "blooming, exuberant", l. 960) force of his μανίας (_manias_, "madness", l. 958) trickles off, ἀποστάζει (_apostazei_). It is _deinos_ again, of a human fury that is drained by confinement. Imprisonment cures Lycurgus. Antigone is not held long enough to be cured of anything, and the Chorus said only minutes ago that the same winds still drive her.

s10.quote: ’Twas madness gibes against a god to fling.
s10.note: ἐπέγνω (_epegno_, "he came to know", l. 960). Lycurgus learned, in his prison, what he had done. That is the thing Antigone in [[s9]] said she would do if the gods judged against her, and the thing Creon does at the end, too late. The participle is ψαύων (_psauon_, "touching, laying hold of", l. 961): he touched the god with jeering tongues. Antigone used the same verb when she told the elders they had touched her sorest wound. Within minutes Creon will be scoffing at Zeus's eagles to Teiresias's face.

s10.quote: For once he fain had quenched the Maenad’s fire;
s10.note: He tried to stop the ἐνθέους γυναῖκας (_entheous gynaikas_, "women with the god in them", l. 962) and the Bacchic fire, and provoked the Μούσας (_Mousas_, "Muses", l. 965). A king suppressing women who act for a god: the application to Creon is hard to miss, and it uses the play's charged word _gyne_. Notice also what kind of offence it is. Lycurgus sinned against worship, song and celebration. Creon forbade a lament and has just sneered at songs and wailing.

s10.quote: By the Iron Rocks that guard the double main,
s10.note: The third story moves to the far north-east edge of the Greek world: the Dark Rocks at the mouth of the Bosporus, and Salmydessus on the Thracian coast, which the Greek calls ἄξενος (_axenos_, "hostile to strangers", l. 967). The savagery of the setting is deliberate. So is the obscurity: the ode never names Phineus's wife or the stepmother, and Sophocles' audience, who knew the tale, are left to supply it. We have to piece it together.

s10.quote: There on his borders Ares witnessed
s10.note: Ares is ἀγχίπτολις (_anchiptolis_, "neighbour to the city", l. 970), a god who lives next door and watches. He does not intervene. Polis-compounds in this play usually carry weight (_hypsipolis_ and _apolis_ in [[s4]]), and here the god nearest the city is the god of violence, a spectator at a crime inside a household. That is a fair picture of what the gods have been in Thebes so far today.

s10.quote: The vengeance by a jealous step-dame ta’en
s10.note: King Phineus had two sons by Cleopatra, put her aside and took a second wife, who blinded the boys. Storr's 'jealous step-dame' is ἀγρίας δάμαρτος (_agrias damartos_, "a savage wife", l. 973). The wound is ἀρατὸν ἕλκος (_araton helkos_, "an accursed wound", l. 972), close kin to the word Antigone used when she called herself accursed in [[s9]]. Some versions say Cleopatra was imprisoned, which would complete the pattern, but the ode does not say so, and its interest has shifted from the prisoner to mutilated children.

s10.quote: The gore that trickled from a spindle red,
s10.note: κερκίδων (_kerkidon_, "shuttles", l. 976): the weapon is a weaving tool, the emblem of women's work indoors, in bloodied hands. A household instrument turned on the household's own children is this family tragedy in small. It also looks ahead. The play's last death is a wife's, inside the house, with a blade at the altar, cursing her husband for their sons.

s10.quote: The sightless orbits of her step-sons twain.
s10.note: The eye-sockets are ἀλαστόροισιν (_alastoroisin_, l. 974), a word from _alastor_, the avenging spirit: the blinded eyes cry out for vengeance. Why end an ode for Antigone with blinded boys? One reason is on its way down the road. The next figure to enter, on a boy's arm, is the blind Teiresias, and his first words are about two seeing with the eyes of one. Blindness that sees, and sight that does not, is where the play goes next.

s10.quote: Wasting away they mourned their piteous doom,
s10.note: τακόμενοι (_takomenoi_, "wasting, melting", l. 977) is Niobe's verb from [[s9]], the one Antigone chose for her own likeness. The elders refused her that comparison when she made it, and now they give its key word to the sons of Cleopatra. The boys do what she did throughout the kommos: they weep for themselves because no one else will.

s10.quote: The blasted issue of their mother’s womb.
s10.note: Storr's 'blasted issue' flattens a pointed phrase: ἀνύμφευτον γονάν (_anympheuton gonan_, "a birth from an unbridal marriage", l. 980), meaning their mother's marriage was a disaster. It is the vocabulary of Antigone's lament, unwed and without wedding song, and of her cry over her own mother's marriage bed. Children ruined by the marriage that made them describes her as well as it describes them.

s10.quote: To great Erecththeus’ race;
s10.note: 'Erecththeus' is a misprint for Erechtheus. Cleopatra's mother was Oreithyia, daughter of the Athenian king Erechtheus, whom the north wind Boreas carried off, so she is of the Ἐρεχθεϊδᾶν (_Erechtheidan_, "the sons of Erechtheus", l. 982), which is a poetic name for the Athenians themselves. For the audience this is the one prisoner in the ode who is their own. Athens honoured Boreas with a cult after the storms that wrecked the Persian fleet.

s10.quote: Swift as his horses o’er the hills she sped;
s10.note: After two stanzas of dark the ode opens for a moment into pure speed: the daughter of Boreas, Βορεὰς (_Boreas_, l. 985), reared in far-off caves among her father's storms, ἅμιππος (_hamippos_, "keeping pace with horses") over the steep hills. She is a creature of open air, which makes what happened to her the sharpest contrast in the ode. The cave and the storm wind also gather up the imagery fastened on Antigone, the rock chamber and the gusts of the soul.

s10.quote: A child of gods; yet she, my child, like thee,
s10.note: θεῶν παῖς (_theon pais_, "child of gods", l. 986), and then ὦ παῖ (_o pai_, "child", l. 987) to Antigone: the same noun for the goddess's daughter and the condemned girl. In [[s9]] the elders told her she was mortal and Niobe divine, and refused the comparison. Now they make one like it themselves. The address has softened from the 'self-willed' of the kommos, and the whole moral, such as it is, is here: even the granddaughter of a god was overtaken.

s10.quote: That knows not death nor age—she too was vanquished.
s10.note: The Μοῖραι μακραίωνες (_Moirai makraiones_, "the long-lived Fates", l. 987) bore down on her too. So what do the three have in common with Antigone? High birth, a prison, and a power no one resists. And what not? Danae was visited by a god and released. Lycurgus was guilty and came to know it. Cleopatra's story is about a cruel marriage, where Antigone has none at all. None of them is said to die in the prison, and none chose her fate, where Antigone, _autonomos_, chose hers. By calling it all destiny the ode avoids naming the one person present who could still open the tomb. Teiresias, entering now, names him.
